title: Stop Fine-Tuning to Fix Retrieval Problems — Anant Srivastava
talk_summary: The speaker argues prompt, memory, and weights are separate tools: prompts hold stable behavior, memory holds current/large/citable facts, and fine-tuning is only for stable reflexes or cost. The practical diagnostic is rate of change, size, and access scope, with a feedback loop moving repeated patterns from context to memory and eventually to weights.

takeaways.what_they_do: Keep prompts for stable behavior, tone, persona, and authored instructions; move large or changing facts out of the prompt into retrieval or memory.
takeaways.evidence_quote: The wrong job for the prompt is to store facts.

takeaways.what_they_do: Decide prompt vs memory vs weights by whether knowledge is large, changing faster than retraining, and scoped by user/repo/access.
takeaways.evidence_quote: knowledge that is current, large and citable

takeaways.what_they_do: For code retrieval, chunk code-aware and attach metadata such as repo and access scope, then filter before returning chunks to avoid irrelevant context.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you need to make sure that you are chunking properly you are using code aware chunking

takeaways.what_they_do: Do not stuff large product catalogs or documentation into prompts; retrieve only relevant facts when needed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You don't put product catalog into the prompt because you are unnecessarily providing context to your model and paying the cost for it.

takeaways.what_they_do: Treat prompt/context, memory, and weights as a loop: repeated successful patterns become durable memory or reflexes, reducing what must be retrieved each time.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the agent gets better at its job by the virtue of doing its job.

takeaways.what_they_do: When an agent gives wrong answers, first check whether it received the right chunks rather than changing the model or fine-tuning.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If the model was not giving the right answer, what the model needed was the right chunks
